Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, an army is diverse, and its elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers produce the one result; they conquer an opposing army in battle, in the same way, your majesty, these mental states, though being diverse, produce the one result; they kill the defilements.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Production of One Result from Various Mental States Question sixteenth Great Chapter first In this chapter sixteen questions

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the one who arises the same or otherwise?” The elder said, “Neither the same, nor otherwise.” “Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, when you were a child, young and tender and lying on your back, were you the same as you are now that you are grown?” “Certainly not, venerable sir. That child, young and tender and lying on his back was one thing, and I now grown am another.” “That being so, your majesty, there would be no notion of mother, nor of father, nor of teacher, nor of a craftsperson, nor of a virtuous person, nor of a wise person. Can it be, your majesty, that the mother of the embryo is different from the mother at the next foetal stage, which is different from the mother of following foetal stages, that the mother of a child is different from the mother of the grown person, that one who trains in a craft is different from the one who is trained, that the one who commits an evil deed is different from the one whose hands and feet are cut off?” “Certainly not, venerable sir. And what would you say if somebody said this to be so?” The elder said, “It was just I, your majesty, who was a child, young and tender and lying on my back, and now it is just I who has grown, and all these states are held together dependent on just this body.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person might light a lamp, might it stay lit all night?” “Yes, venerable sir, it might stay lit all night.” “Is it so, your majesty, that the flame in the first watch of the night is the same as that in the middle watch?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Is the flame in the middle watch of the night the same as that in the last watch?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Is it then so, your majesty, that the lamp in the first watch of the night is different from that in the middle watch, which is different from that in the last watch?” “Certainly not, venerable sir. It was burning all through the night dependent on just itself.” “In the same way, your majesty, a continuity of states runs on; as one arises, another ceases. It runs on like there was no before and no after. Consequently, it is neither the same nor the other and the last consciousness is comprised of the first consciousness.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, milk some time after being milked from a cow would turn to curds, and from curds into butter, and from butter to ghee, would someone who might say, ‘That milk is those curds, those curds is that butter, that butter is that ghee,’ be speaking rightly?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, they come into being because of it.” “In the same way, your majesty, a continuity of states runs on; as one arises, another ceases. It runs on like there was no before and no after. Consequently, it is neither the same nor the other and the last consciousness is comprised of the first consciousness.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Continuity of States Question first

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does someone who does not reconnect know ‘I will not reconnect’?” “Yes, your majesty, someone who does not reconnect knows ‘I will not reconnect’.” “How do they know, venerable sir?” “From the cessation, your majesty, of the cause and condition for reconnecting one knows ‘I will not reconnect’.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just like, your majesty, a householder farmer, having ploughed and sown might fill his grain house. But then, after some time, he would not plough and sow, and would use up the grain he had stored, or dispose of it, or deal with it according to conditions, would that householder farmer know, your majesty, ‘I will not fill my grain house’?” “Yes, venerable sir, he would know.” “How would he know?” “From the cessation of that cause and condition for filling the grain house one knows ‘I will not fill my grain house’.” “In the same way, your majesty, from the cessation of the cause and condition for reconnecting one knows ‘I will not reconnect’.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Reconnection Question second

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, would wisdom also have arisen?” “Yes, your majesty, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, wisdom also has arisen.” “What, venerable sir, is knowledge the same as wisdom?” “Yes, your majesty, knowledge is the same as wisdom.” “Then, venerable sir, for one in whom knowledge has arisen which is the same as wisdom, would he be confused or would he not be confused?” “He would be confused in some instances, your majesty, and would not be confused in other instances.” “When, venerable sir, would he be confused?” “He would be confused, your majesty, concerning those aspects of a craft that he did not know before, or those directions in which he has not gone before, or those names and designations he has not heard before.” “When, venerable sir, would he not be confused?” “He would not be confused, your majesty, concerning that which he has discerned by wisdom, that is, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self.” “Then where, venerable sir, does his confusion go?” “Confusion ceases, your majesty, at that very moment when knowledge arises.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person might bring in a lamp to a dark house, then the darkness ceases, and light appears. In the same way, your majesty, at the moment when knowledge arises, right there confusion ceases.” “Then where, venerable sir, does wisdom go?” “Wisdom, your majesty, ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.” “Venerable Nāgasena, what you have just said, ‘Wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease,’ please make an analogy for that.” “Just as, your majesty, some person, wishing to send a letter at night, would summon a scribe and light a lamp, and have the letter written. Then, when the letter is written, he would extinguish the lamp. And when the lamp is extinguished the letter would not be destroyed. In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, people in the eastern districts might set up five water pots in each house so as to extinguish any burning, and when a house is on fire, they would throw these five pots of water on top of the house, then the fire would be extinguished. Would it occur to these people, your majesty, ‘We must make use of these pots again’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, those pots have done their job, what further need would there be for them?” “As, your majesty, are the five pots of water, so the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are to be seen. As those people, so the spiritual practitioner is to be seen. As the fire, so the defilements are to be seen. As the fire is extinguished by the five pots of water, so the defilements are extinguished by the five faculties, and those extinguished defilements do not arise again. In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a doctor, having taken the five root medicines and approached a sick person, might crush the five root medicines and get the sick person to drink them, and the sickness would disappear. Would it occur to that doctor, your majesty, ‘I will make use of the five root medicines again’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, those five root medicines have done their job, what further need would there be for them?” “As, your majesty, are the five root medicines, so the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are to be seen. As the doctor, so the spiritual practitioner is to be seen. As the disease, so the defilements are to be seen. As the sick person, so the common person is to be seen. As the disease of the sick person is expelled by the five root medicines such that when the disease is expelled the sick person becomes well, so the defilements are expelled by the five faculties, and those expelled defilements do not arise again. In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a warrior, skilled in battle, having taken five arrows and entered into battle in order to defeat an opposing army, and gone into battle he might let fly those five arrows, and the opposing army is destroyed by them. Would it occur to that warrior, skilled in battle, your majesty, ‘I will make use of these five arrows again’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, those five arrows have done their job, what further need would there be for them?” “As, your majesty, are the five arrows, so the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are to be seen. As the warrior, skilled in battle, so the spiritual practitioner is to be seen. As the opposing army, so the defilements are to be seen. As the opposing army is destroyed by the five arrows, so the defilements are destroyed by the five faculties, and those destroyed defilements do not arise again. In the same way, your majesty, wisdom ceases right there having done its task, but that understood by wisdom, the notions of impermanent, suffering, and not self do not cease.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Knowledge and Wisdom Question third

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does one who does not reconnect feel a painful feeling?” The elder said: “He feels some, and he does not feel others.” “Which does he feel, and which does he not feel?” “He feels bodily feelings, your majesty, and he does not feel mental feelings.” “How, venerable sir, does he feel bodily feelings, and how does he not feel mental feelings?” “There is no ceasing of that cause and condition for the arising of a painful bodily feeling, and thus he feels a painful bodily feeling. There is ceasing of that cause and condition for the arising of a painful mental feeling, and thus he does not feel a painful mental feeling. And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One: ‘He only feels one feeling, the bodily one, not the mental.’” “Venerable Nāgasena, why does one who feels a painful feeling not experience final nibbāna?” “For an arahant, your majesty, there is no delight nor repugnance, and arahants do not destroy what is unripe. The wise ones wait for full maturing. And this too was said, your majesty, by the elder Sāriputta, the general of the Dhamma: ‘I don’t delight in dying, nor do I delight in living. But I wait for the right time, as a servant waits for his wages. I don’t delight in dying, nor do I delight in living. But I wait for the right time, clearly comprehending and fully mindful.’” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Feelings of an Individual Reconnecting fourth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is pleasant feeling wholesome or unwholesome or indeterminate?” “It could be wholesome, your majesty, or it could be unwholesome, or it could be indeterminate.” “If, venerable sir, wholesome feelings are not painful, and if painful feelings are not wholesome, then there does not arise a wholesome feeling which is painful.” “What do you think, your majesty, if one might place a hot iron ball in a man’s hand and place a snowball in his other hand, would both hurt him?” “Yes, venerable sir, they would both hurt him.” “Well, your majesty, are they both hot?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “What then, your majesty, are they both cold?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Know your own refutation. If something hot hurts, and they are not both hot, it is not because of that the suffering arises. And, if something cold hurts, and they are not both cold, it is not because of that the suffering arises. So, how is it, your majesty, that both hurt, and they are not both hot, and they are not both cold? And, how is it that with one hot and the other cold, they both hurt, and it is not because of that the suffering arises?” “I am not competent to converse with you, a debater of the doctrine. It would be good, venerable sir, if you told me the meaning.” Then the elder instructed King Milinda with a talk connected with Abhidhamma. “There are, your majesty, these six joys dependent on the householder life, these six joys dependent on renunciation, these six sorrows dependent on the householder life, these six sorrows dependent on renunciation, these six neutral feelings dependent on the householder life, these six neutral feelings dependent on renunciation. Thus, there are these six sets of six. There are then thirty-six types of feeling in the past, thirty-six types of feeling in the future, and thirty-six types of feeling in the present. So, assembling them and bringing them all together, there are one hundred and eight types of feeling.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Feelings Question fifth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, what reconnects?” The elder said: “Name-and-form, your majesty, reconnects.” “Does this very name-and-form reconnect?” “This very name-and-form, your majesty, does not reconnect. With this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects.” “If, venerable sir, this very name-and-form does not reconnect, is it not then that it would be freed from evil actions?” The elder said: “If it would not reconnect, then it would be freed from evil actions. But because, your majesty, it does reconnect, it therefore is not freed from evil actions.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might steal another person’s mangos, and the mango owner might grab that person and point him out to the king, saying ‘My mangos have been stolen by this man.’ And he might say ‘Lord, I did not steal this person’s mangos. Those mangos I took are not the same as those that this person planted; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would that man, your majesty, deserve punishment?” “Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.” “For what reason?” “Whatever he might say, venerable sir, while not disavowing the earlier mangos, he would be deserving of punishment due to the later mangos.” “In the same way, your majesty, with this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might steal another person’s rice, … sugar-cane … Just as, your majesty, some person or other might light a fire during the wintertime, and warm himself, and might leave without having extinguished it, and that fire might burn another person’s field. And the owner of the field might grab that person and point him out to the king, saying ‘My field has been burned by this man.’ And he might say ‘Lord, I did not set fire to this person’s field. The fire I did not extinguish was not the same as the fire that burned this person’s field; I do not deserve punishment.’ Would that man, your majesty, deserve punishment?” “Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.” “For what reason?” “Whatever he might say, venerable sir, while not disavowing the earlier fire, he would be deserving of punishment by means of the later fire.” “In the same way, your majesty, with this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other, having taken a lamp and ascended to the top of a mansion, might use it, and the burning lamp might set fire to the roof thatch, and the burning thatch might set fire to the house, and the burning house might set fire to the village, and the villagers, having seized that man, might say, ‘Why, sir, did you set fire to the village?’ And he might say ‘I did not, friend, set fire to the village. The fire in the lamp whose light I enjoyed was not the same as the fire that burned the village.’ And if they were to come before you while arguing, whose side of the argument, your majesty, would you support?” “That of the villagers, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Since, whatever he might say, this fire was produced just from that one.” “In the same way, your majesty, whatever name-and form that has death as its end, another name-and-form is in reconnection, and it was produced just from that one. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other, having contracted for a young girl in marriage and having paid the bride price, might leave. Then, after some time, she would reach full marriageable age, then another man, having paid the bride price would lead her away in marriage. The former man would come and say, ‘Why, sir, have you led away my wife?’ And he might say ‘I have not led away your wife. The young girl for whom you have contracted and paid the bride price is not the same as the young woman who has attained marriageable age and been contracted for and paid for by me.’ And if they were to come before you while arguing, whose side of the argument, your majesty, would you support?” “That of the former man, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Since, whatever he might say, this grown woman was produced just from that one.” “In the same way, your majesty, whatever name-and form that has death as its end, another name-and-form is in reconnection, and it was produced just from that one. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other, having bought a pot of milk from the hand of a cowherd, might put it in his care and leave, saying, ‘I will come back for it tomorrow,’ and that milk would become curds. Then, he might come back and say ‘Give me my pot of milk.’ And the cowherd would show him the curds. The other would then say, ‘I did not buy curds from you, give me my pot of milk.’ Then, that one would say, ‘Without you knowing it, the milk has become curds.’ And if they were to come before you while arguing, whose side of the argument, your majesty, would you support?” “That of the cowherd, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Since, whatever he might say, this one was produced just from that one.” “In the same way, your majesty, whatever name-and form that has death as its end, another name-and-form is in reconnection, and it was produced just from that one. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Identity or Difference of Name-and-Form sixth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, will you then reconnect?” “Enough, your majesty, why are you asking this? Have I not declared to you previously, ‘If, your majesty, I am with clinging I will reconnect, and if I am without clinging I will not reconnect’?” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might perform a service for the king, and the king, satisfied, would repay that service. And that person, because of that service, would go about provided with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, and might announce to the populace, ‘The king does not do anything for me.’ Would that man, your majesty, be acting rightly?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, why are you asking this? Have I not declared to you previously, ‘If I am with clinging I will reconnect, and if I am without clinging I will not reconnect’?” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Elder’s Reconnection or Non-Reconnection seventh

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, you talked then of name-and-form. What in there is name, and what is form?” “Whatever in there, your majesty, is gross, that is form. Whatever in there are subtle mental states that are mental factors in the mind, that is name.” “Venerable Nāgasena, why doesn’t just name alone reconnect, nor form alone?” “These things, your majesty, are mutually dependent and they only arise together.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, there could not be just a yolk nor just an egg-shell, since the yoke and the egg-shell are both mutually dependent and they only arise together. In the same way, your majesty, if there were no name there would be no form, and what name there is and what form there is, these are both mutually dependent and they only arise together. Thus, there is this long extent of transmigration time.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Reconnection of Name-and-form eighth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, you talked then of a long extent of transmigration time. What is this thing called transmigration time?” “The past, your majesty, is transmigration time, the future is transmigration time, the present is transmigration time.” “But, venerable sir, does all transmigration time exist?” “Some transmigration time exists, your majesty, and some does not.” “What then, venerable sir, exists and what does not?” “Those mental formations, your majesty, that are past, gone, ceased, and changed, that transmigration time does not exist. Those mental formations that have reached fruition, or have the nature to be liable for fruition, or those that give reconnection elsewhere, that transmigration time does exist. Those beings that have died and arisen elsewhere, that transmigration time does exist. Those beings that have died and not arisen elsewhere, that transmigration time does not exist. And those beings that have attained final nibbāna, that transmigration time does not exist because of the attainment of nibbāna.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Time Question ninth Time Chapter second In this chapter nine questions

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the root of transmigration time in the past, what is the root of transmigration time in the future, what is the root of transmigration time in the present?” “The root of transmigration time in the past, your majesty, and of transmigration time in the future, and of transmigration time in the present is ignorance. From the condition of ignorance there are fabrications, from the condition of fabrications there is consciousness, from the condition of consciousness there is name-and-form, from the condition of name-and-form there are the six sense bases, from the condition of the six sense bases there is contact, from the condition of contact there is feeling, from the condition of feeling there is craving, from the condition of craving there is clinging, from the condition of clinging there is becoming, from the condition of becoming there is birth, from the condition of birth there is old age and death; sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair arise. Thus, no earliest point of this whole mass of suffering of transmigration time can be discerned.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Root of Time first

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, concerning that which you said, ‘No earliest point can be discerned,’ please give me an analogy for that.” “Just as, your majesty, a man might put a small seed in the ground, then it having produced a sprout and having gradually undergone increase, growth, and full maturity, it would ripen into fruit. Then again having taken from that a seed and cultivated it, then it having produced a sprout and having gradually undergone increase, growth, and full maturity, it would ripen into fruit. Is there thus an end to this continuity?” “There is not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, no earliest point of transmigration time can be discerned.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, an egg might be produced from a hen, a hen from that egg, and an egg from that hen, and so on. Is there thus an end to this continuity?” “There is not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, no earliest point of transmigration time can be discerned.” “Give me another analogy.” The elder drew a circle on the ground and said to King Milinda, “Is there an end to this circle?” “There is not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, these cycles spoken of by the Blessed One, ‘Dependent on the eye and form, eye consciousness arises, and the meeting of the three is contact. From the condition of contact there is feeling, from the condition of feeling there is craving, from the condition of craving there is clinging, from the condition of clinging there is kamma, and again the eye is born from kamma.’ Is there thus an end to this continuity?” “There is not, venerable sir.” “‘Dependent on the ear and sound … Dependent on the mind and thought, mind consciousness arises, and the meeting of the three is contact. From the condition of contact there is feeling, from the condition of feeling there is craving, from the condition of craving there is clinging, from the condition of clinging there is kamma, and again the mind is born from kamma.’ Is there thus an end to this continuity?” “There is not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, no earliest point of transmigration time can be discerned.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Earliest Point second

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, concerning that which you said, ‘No earliest point can be discerned,’ what is this earliest point?” “That which is time in the past, your majesty, is the earliest point.” “Venerable Nāgasena, concerning that which you said, ‘No earliest point can be discerned,’ is it that all earliest points cannot be discerned?” “Some can be discerned, your majesty, and some cannot be.” “What can be discerned, venerable sir, and what cannot?” “That earliest point cannot be discerned, your majesty, where earlier than this no ignorance was existing at all, by any means, or in any way. That which having not existed arose, and having existed disappeared again, that earliest point can be discerned.” “Venerable Nāgasena, that which having not existed arose, and having existed disappeared again would it not, having been cut off at both ends, be entirely destroyed?” “If, your majesty, having been cut off at both ends, it was entirely destroyed, is it possible, being cut off at both ends, to grow?” “Yes, it is possible for it to grow. I am not asking that, venerable sir; is it possible for it to grow from that end?” “Yes, it is possible for it to grow.” “Please give me an analogy.” The elder made him an analogy of a tree, “The aggregates are the seeds of this whole mass of suffering.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Discernment of an End Point third

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, are there any fabrications which are produced?” “Yes, your majesty, there are fabrications which are produced.” “What are they, venerable sir?” “When there is the eye and forms, your majesty, there is eye consciousness. When there is eye consciousness, there is eye contact. When there is eye contact, there is feeling. When there is feeling, there is craving. When there is craving, there is becoming. When there is becoming, there is birth. When there is birth, there is old age and death, and sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair come to be. Thus, there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. When there is no eye and forms, your majesty, there is no eye consciousness. When there is no eye consciousness, there is no eye contact. When there is no eye contact, there is no feeling. When there is no feeling, there is no craving. When there is no craving, there is no becoming. When there is no becoming, there is no birth. When there is no birth, there is no old age and death, and there is no sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair. Thus, there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Production of Fabrications fourth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, are there any fabrications which are produced without development?” “Your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, was this house that you are sitting in produced without development?” “There is nothing here, venerable sir, produced without development; it is produced only with development. These pieces of wood were in the forest, and this clay was in the ground, and thus this house was produced by the appropriate effort of women and men.” “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, whatever seeds and plants thrown on the ground gradually attain to growth, development, and maturity, and would give flowers and fruit, no trees would be produced without development, and trees would only be produced with development.” “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a potter might take clay from the ground and make various bowls, those bowls are not produced without development, and bowls would only be produced with development.” “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as if, your majesty, there were no sound-board for a lute, no parchment, no belly, no arm, no neck, no strings, no plectrum, and no suitable effort from a person, would sound be produced?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “But if, your majesty, there were a sound-board for a lute, parchment, a belly, an arm, a neck, strings, a plectrum, and suitable effort from a person, would sound be produced?” “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as if, your majesty, there were no lower piece of wood, no twirling stick, no string for the twirling stick, no upper piece of wood, no bark, and no suitable effort from a person, would fire be produced?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “But if, your majesty, there were a lower piece of wood, a twirling stick, string for the twirling stick, an upper piece of wood, bark, and suitable effort from a person, would fire be produced?” “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as if, your majesty, there were no crystal glass, no heat, and no cow-dung, would fire be produced?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “But if, your majesty, there were a crystal glass, heat, and cow-dung, would fire be produced?” “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “Give me another analogy.” “Just as if, your majesty, there were no mirror, no light, and no face, would an image be produced?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “But if, your majesty, there were a mirror, light, and a face, would an image be produced?” “Yes, it would be produced, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, there are no fabrications which are produced without development. Fabrications are only produced with development.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Production and Development of Fabrications fifth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is an experiencer to be found?” “But what then is this thing called an experiencer?” “That soul within, venerable sir, that sees a form with the eye, hears a sound with the ear, smells an odour with the nose, tastes a flavour with the tongue, touches a tangible with the body, and knows a thought with the mind, just as we, seated here in the palace, might look out of whichever window we wish to look out of – whether that be the east, the west, the north, or the south window. Even so, venerable sir, this soul within looks out of whatever door it wishes to look out of.” The elder said: “I will talk to you, your majesty, about the five doors. Listen to this and pay careful attention. If the soul within sees form with the eye, just as we, sitting here in the palace can see material form through whatever window we wish to look through, whether through the east, the west, the north, or the south window, could a material form be seen by this soul within by means of the ear, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the body, or by the mind? And could a sound be heard by means of the eye, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the body, or by the mind? And could an odour be smelled by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the tongue, or by the body, or by the mind? And could a flavour be tasted by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the nose, or by the body, or by the mind? And could a tangible be felt by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the mind? And could a thought be known by means of the eye, or by the ear, or by the nose, or by the tongue, or by the body?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter. Just as, your majesty, when these grilled windows are removed, we seated here in the palace, looking outward, see form more clearly through great space, would the soul within see form more clearly through great space when the doors of the eyes have been removed? ... when the ears have been removed? ... when the nose has been removed? ... when the tongue has been removed? And would it feel a tangible more clearly when the body has been removed?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter. Just as if, your majesty, this Dinna were to depart and stand in the entrance way outside the door, would you know ‘this Dinna has departed and is standing in the entrance way outside the door’?” “Yes, venerable sir, I would know.” “And then, just as if, your majesty, this Dinna were to come back inside and stand in front of you, would you know ‘this Dinna has come back inside and is standing in front of me’?” “Yes, venerable sir, I would know.” “In the same way, your majesty, when a flavour is placed on the tongue, would the soul within know whether its essence were sour, salty, bitter, pungent, astringent, or sweet?” “Yes, venerable sir, it would know.” “And when it has gone from your tongue into your inside would it know whether its essence were sour, salty, bitter, pungent, astringent, or sweet?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter. Just as if, your majesty, some person or other might fetch a hundred pots of honey, fill a large trough with this honey, cover the mouth of a man, and throw him into the trough of honey, would that man know whether the honey were sweet or not?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable sir, the honey has not entered his mouth.” “The latter is not fitted to the former, your majesty, nor the former to the latter.” “I am not competent to converse with you, a debater of the doctrine. It would be good, venerable sir, if you told me the meaning.” The elder instructed King Milinda with a talk connected with Abhidhamma. “Here, your majesty, dependent on the eye and form, eye consciousness arises, and from the coming together of that there is contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, the life faculty, and attention. Thus, these things are produced from conditions, and no experiencer is found here. Dependent on the ear and sounds … dependent on the mind and thoughts, mind consciousness arises, and from the coming together of that there is contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, the life faculty, and attention. Thus, these things are produced from conditions, and no experiencer is found here.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Experiencer sixth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does mind consciousness arise where eye consciousness arises?” “Yes, your majesty, mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises.” “Venerable Nāgasena, does eye consciousness arise first, then mind consciousness after, or does mind consciousness arise first, then eye consciousness after?” “Eye consciousness arises first, your majesty, then mind consciousness arises after.” “Venerable Nāgasena, does eye consciousness instruct mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ or does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’?” “Certainly not, your majesty, there is no conversation between them.” “Then, how is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises?” “It is because of inclination, your majesty, and because of door, of habit, and of practice.” “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of inclination mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises? Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, when it is raining what way would the water go?” “It would go according to the inclination, venerable sir.” “And if it would continue to rain for some time, what way would that water go?” “It would go in the same direction as the earlier water, venerable sir.” “Does the earlier water, your majesty, instruct the later water, ‘where I go, you should go,’ or does the later water instruct the earlier water ‘where you will go, there I will go’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, there is no conversation between them, they go because of the inclination.” “In the same way, your majesty, because of the inclination eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of the inclination.” “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of door mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises? Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty? There might be a king’s border town with strong ramparts, an arched gateway, and only one door, and there, if a man were wishing to depart, how would he do so?” “He would depart through the door, venerable sir.” “Then, if there was another man wishing to depart, how would he do so?” “He would depart in the same way as the first man, venerable sir.” “Does the first man, your majesty, instruct the later man, ‘where I go, you should go,’ or does the later man instruct the first man ‘where you will go, there I will go’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, there is no conversation between them, they go because of the door.” “In the same way, your majesty, because of the door eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of the door.” “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of habit mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises? Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty? If one cart goes first, then which way would a second cart go?” “It would go in the same way as the first cart, venerable sir.” “Does the first cart, your majesty, instruct the later cart, ‘where I go, you should go,’ or does the later cart instruct the first cart ‘where you will go, there I will go’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, there is no conversation between them, they go because of habit.” “In the same way, your majesty, because of habit eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of habit.” “How is it, Venerable Nāgasena, that because of practice mind consciousness arises where eye consciousness arises? Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a beginner might be clumsy in the arts of hand reckoning, calculation, mental reckoning, and writing, but then, after some time, with careful working and practice, he would become skilful. In the same way, your majesty, because of practice eye consciousness arises, then mind consciousness arises. And not because eye consciousness instructs mind consciousness, ‘where I arise, you should arise,’ nor does mind consciousness instruct eye consciousness ‘where you will arise, there I will arise’. There is no conversation between them, they arise because of practice.” “Venerable Nāgasena, does mind consciousness arise where ear consciousness arises? ... where nose consciousness arises … where tongue consciousness arises … where body consciousness arises?” “Yes, your majesty, mind consciousness arises where body consciousness arises.” “Venerable Nāgasena, does body consciousness arise first, then mind consciousness after, or does mind consciousness arise first, then body consciousness after?” “Body consciousness arises first, your majesty, then mind consciousness arises after.” “Venerable Nāgasena, does … there is no conversation between them, they arise because of practice.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Eye Consciousness, Etc. seventh

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, do contact and also feeling arise where mind consciousness arises?” “Yes, your majesty, where mind consciousness arises, there too contact, feeling, perception, intention, applied thought, and examination arise, and all mental states that arise there are led by contact.” “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of contact?” “Touching, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of contact.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Suppose, your majesty, that two rams were fighting. One of these rams is to be seen as the eye, the other ram is to be seen as form, and the meeting of the two is to be seen as contact.” “Give me another analogy.” “Suppose, your majesty, that two hands were clapped together. One of these hands is to be seen as the eye, the other hand is to be seen as form, and the meeting of the two is to be seen as contact.” “Give me another analogy.” “Suppose, your majesty, that two cymbals were clanged together. One of these cymbals is to be seen as the eye, the other cymbal is to be seen as form, and the meeting of the two is to be seen as contact.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Distinguishing Characteristic of Contact Question eighth

“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of feeling?” “Being felt and experiencing, your majesty, are the distinguishing characteristics of feeling.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might perform a service for the king, and the king, satisfied, would repay that service. And that person, because of that service, would go about provided with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, and it might occur to him ‘previously I performed a service for the king and he, satisfied, repaid me for that service, and for that reason I experience such and such feelings.’ Or just as, your majesty, some person or other might perform a good deed and at the beak up of the body after dying, might be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, and there would go about provided with and possessed of the five strands of divine sensual pleasure, and it might occur to him ‘previously I performed a good deed, and for that reason I experience such and such feelings.’ In the same way, your majesty, being felt and experiencing are the distinguishing characteristics of feeling.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Distinguishing Characteristic of Feeling Question ninth

“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of perception?” “Perceiving, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of perception. What does one perceive? One perceives blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson. Thus, your majesty, perceiving is the distinguishing characteristic of perception.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a king’s storekeeper, having entered the warehouse and seen the forms of the king’s goods there, perceives blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson. Thus, your majesty, perceiving is the distinguishing characteristic of perception.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Distinguishing Characteristic of Perception Question tenth

“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of intention?” “Willing and arranging, your majesty, are the distinguishing characteristics of intention.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might prepare a poison and drink it himself and get others to drink it, then he himself would become afflicted and others would become afflicted. In the same way, your majesty, some person here, through intention, would will an unwholesome action and on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a bad destination, a state of suffering, a hell realm. And those who followed him, on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a bad destination, a state of suffering, a hell realm. Or just as, your majesty, some person or other might prepare a mixture of ghee, butter, oil, honey and molasses and drink it himself and get others to drink it, then he himself would become happy and others would become happy. In the same way, your majesty, some person here, through intention, would will a wholesome action and on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly realm. And those who followed him, on the break up of the body, after dying, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly realm. So too, your majesty, willing and arranging are the distinguishing characteristics of intention.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Distinguishing Characteristic of Intention Question eleventh

“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of consciousness?” “Knowing, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of consciousness?” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a town guardian sitting in the middle of the crossroads of the town would see a man coming from the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, and the northern direction. In the same way, your majesty, a person knows with consciousness whatever form he sees with his eyes, he knows with consciousness whatever sound he hears with his ears, he knows with consciousness whatever odour he smells with his nose, he knows with consciousness whatever flavour he tastes with his tongue, he knows with consciousness whatever tangible he touches with his body, and he knows with consciousness whatever thought he knows with his mind. So too, your majesty, knowing is the distinguishing characteristic of consciousness?” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Distinguishing Characteristic of Consciousness Question twelfth

“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of applied thought?” “Mental fixing, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of applied thought.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a carpenter fixes a superbly crafted piece of wood into a join, in the same way mental fixing is the distinguishing characteristic of applied thought.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Distinguishing Characteristic of Applied Thought Question thirteenth

“Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinguishing characteristic of examination?” “Continuity, your majesty, is the distinguishing characteristic of examination.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, a bronze bowl which has been struck resounds afterwards, and lingers on, applied thought is to be seen as striking, examination is to be seen as resounding.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Distinguishing Characteristic of Examination Question fourteenth Examination Chapter third In this chapter fourteen questions

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible, having repeatedly analysed these mental states that are of the nature to arise together, to declare a difference between them, saying ‘this is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is intention, this is consciousness, this is applied thought, this is examination’?” “No, your majesty, it is not possible to do that.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as if, your majesty, a king’s cook might prepare a soup or sauce and put in it curds, salt, ginger, cumin, hot pepper, and various other things, and the king might say ‘bring me a taste of curds, a taste of salt, a taste of ginger, a taste of cumin, a taste of hot pepper, or a taste of all the other things put in.’ Is it possible, your majesty, having repeatedly analysed these tastes that are of the nature to arise together to bring forward an acidic flavour, a salty flavour, a bitter flavour, a sharp flavour, or a pungent flavour, or a sweet flavour?” “It is certainly not possible, venerable sir, to do that.” “In the same way, your majesty, it is not possible, having repeatedly analysed these mental states that are of the nature to arise together, to declare a difference between them, saying ‘this is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is intention, this is consciousness, this is applied thought, this is examination’?” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Analysing Contact, Etc. first

The elder asked: “Is salt, your majesty, cognizable by the eye?” “Yes, venerable sir, it is cognizable by the eye.” “Think carefully, your majesty.” “Is it then, venerable sir, cognizable by the tongue?” “Yes, your majesty, it is cognizable by the tongue.” “Then, venerable sir, is all salt cognizable by the tongue?” “Yes, your majesty, all salt is cognizable by the tongue.” “If, venerable sir, all salt is cognizable by the tongue, why then do oxen bring it by the cartload, shouldn’t just salt be brought?” “It is not possible to bring just salt, your majesty, since these things arise together with a diversity in their range, and as well, salt has heaviness. Is it possible to weigh salt on scales?” “Yes, venerable sir, it is possible.” “It is not possible, your majesty, to weigh salt on scales. One weighs the heaviness on scales.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Nāgasena’s Question second

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, are these five sense bases produced from different kamma or from just one kamma?” “They are produced from different kamma, your majesty, not from just one kamma.” “Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, if one were to sow different seeds in this field, would a diversity of fruits be produced from this diversity of seeds?” “Yes, venerable sir, they would be.” “In the same way, your majesty, these five sense bases are produced from different kamma, and not from just one kamma.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Five Sense Bases Produced from Kamma third

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, why is it that not all people are the same? Some people are short-lived, others long-lived, some have much affliction and others little affliction, some are ugly and others beautiful, some have little power and others great power, some have little wealth and others great wealth, some come from an inferior clan and others from a superior clan, some are foolish and others are wise.” The elder said: “Why then, your majesty, is it that not all trees are the same? Some are acidic, some are salty, some are bitter, some are pungent, some are astringent, and some are sweet?” “I think, venerable sir, that it is because of the difference in seeds.” “In the same way, your majesty, it is because of the difference in kamma that not all people are the same. Some people are short-lived, others long-lived, some have much affliction and others little affliction, some are ugly and others beautiful, some have little power and others great power, some have little wealth and others great wealth, some come from an inferior clan and others from a superior clan, some are foolish and others are wise. And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One: ‘Young man, beings are the owners of their kamma, heirs to their kamma, born from their kamma, bound to their kamma, and protected by their kamma. Kamma divides beings into inferior and superior.’” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Workings of Different Kamma fourth

The king said: “Venerable Nāgasena, you told me that, so that this suffering would cease and another suffering would not arise, that was the goal of your going forth. Is it just because of previous effort? Should not one make an effort at the current time?” The elder said: “Effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful.” “Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, when you become thirsty, would you then have a well or a dam dug and say ‘I will drink water’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful.” “Give me another analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, when you become hungry, would you then have a field ploughed, plant rice, and have the grain brought in, and say ‘I will eat rice’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful.” “Give me another analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, when you are faced with a battle, would you then have a moat dug, a rampart, a gateway, and a watchtower constructed, and then train in the use of elephants, horses, chariots, bows and swords?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, effort at the current time is not so useful, effort made previously is useful. And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One: ‘One should do formerly what one knows is for one’s benefit; Not having thoughts like a wagon driver, one is steadfast in wisdom. As a wagon driver who has abandoned the well-prepared, even, high road, Climbing on the uneven path, just broods with his axle broken, Straying from the Dhamma thus, and following what isn’t Dhamma, The lazy one coming face-to-face with death, just broods with his axle broken.’” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Reason for Effort fifth

The king said: “Venerable Nāgasena, you say that the heat of hell has a far greater intensity than that of a normal fire, and that a small stone placed in a normal fire cooking all day would not be dissolved, whereas a stone the size of a gabled house placed in the fire of hell would be dissolved in a moment. I do not believe this assertion. And then you say that those various beings who have arisen in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved. That assertion too I do not believe.” The elder asked, “What do you think, your majesty, do those female sharks, crocodiles, turtles, pea-hens, and pigeons eat hard stones and gravel?” “Yes, venerable sir, they eat them.” “But then when those have gone down into their abdomens and stomachs are they dissolved?” “Yes, venerable sir, they are dissolved.” “But then is an embryo in their abdomens dissolved?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “I think, venerable sir, due to the workings of kamma it would not dissolve.” “In the same way, your majesty, those various beings in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved. And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One: ‘One does not complete one’s time until there is an end to one’s evil kamma.’” “Give me another analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, do female lions, tigers, panthers, and dogs eat hard bones and flesh?” “Yes, venerable sir, they eat them.” “But then when those have gone down into their abdomens and stomachs are they dissolved?” “Yes, venerable sir, they are dissolved.” “But then is an embryo in their abdomens dissolved?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “I think, venerable sir, due to the workings of kamma it would not dissolve.” “In the same way, your majesty, those various beings in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved.” “Give me another analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, do those delicate Bactrian Greek women, noble women, brahmin women, and householder women eat hard cakes and meat?” “Yes, venerable sir, they eat them.” “But then when those have gone down into their abdomens and stomachs are they dissolved?” “Yes, venerable sir, they are dissolved.” “But then is an embryo in their abdomens dissolved?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “I think, venerable sir, due to the workings of kamma it would not dissolve.” “In the same way, your majesty, those various beings in hell, cooking in that hell for thousands of years are not dissolved. And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One: ‘One does not complete one’s time until there is an end to one’s evil kamma.’” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Nature of Heat in the Fires of Hell sixth

The king said: “Venerable Nāgasena, you say this great earth is established on water, water is established on air, and air is established on space. I do not believe this assertion.” The elder took some water in a water vessel and explained to King Milinda, “Just as, your majesty, this water is supported by the air, so too is that water supported by air.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Bearing Up of the Earth seventh

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is cessation nibbāna?” “Yes, your majesty, cessation is nibbāna.” “How, Venerable Nāgasena, is cessation nibbāna?” “All those foolish ordinary people, your majesty, who delight in the internal and external sense bases, welcome them, remain clinging to them, and are carried away by that stream, are not free from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, anguish, and despair, they are not free from suffering, I say. A well-taught noble disciple, your majesty, does not delight in the internal and external sense bases, nor welcome them, nor remain clinging to them. The one, not delighting in them, not welcoming them, not remaining clinging to them, is free from craving. From the cessation of craving, there is cessation of birth. From the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair cease, and thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. In this way, your majesty, cessation is nibbāna.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Cessation and Nibbāna eighth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does everyone attain nibbāna?” “Not everyone, your majesty, attains nibbāna. Whoever, practicing rightly, directly knows those things which should be directly known, completely comprehends those things that should be completely comprehended, abandons those things that should be abandoned, develops those things that should be developed, personally realises those things that should be personally realised, that one attains nibbāna.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Attaining of Nibbāna ninth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does one who does not attain nibbāna know the happiness of nibbāna?” “Yes, your majesty, one who does not attain nibbāna knows the happiness of nibbāna.” “How, Venerable Nāgasena, not attaining it does one know the happiness of nibbāna?” “What do you think, your majesty, would those who haven’t had their hands and feet cut off know the suffering of having one’s hands and feet cut off?” “Yes, venerable sir, they would know.” “How would they know?” “Having heard, venerable sir, the sounds of lamentation of those who have had their hands and feet cut off, they would know the suffering of having one’s hands and feet cut off.” “In the same way, your majesty, having heard the sound of one who has seen nibbāna, one knows the happiness of nibbāna.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Knowing the Happiness of Nibbāna tenth Nibbāna Chapter fourth In this chapter ten questions

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, have you seen the Buddha?” “Certainly not, your majesty.” “Then, have your teachers seen the Buddha?” “Certainly not, your majesty.” “Therefore, Venerable Nāgasena, there is no Buddha.” “Well then, your majesty, have you seen the River Ūhā in the Himalayas?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Then has your father seen the River Ūhā?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Because of this, your majesty, there is no River Ūhā.” “There is, venerable sir. Even though the River Ūhā has not been seen by me nor by my father, there is a River Ūhā.” “In the same way, your majesty, even though the Blessed One has not been seen by me nor by my teachers, there is a Blessed One.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Existence or Non-existence of the Buddha first

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the Buddha unsurpassed?” “Yes, your majesty, the Blessed One is unsurpassed.” “How, Venerable Nāgasena, do you know the Buddha is unsurpassed if you haven’t seen him before?” “What do you think, your majesty, would those who have not seen the great ocean before know that this great ocean is huge, deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, such that as these five great rivers that flow into it constantly and continually, that is the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī, neither the depletion nor filling up of it is discerned?” “Yes, venerable sir, they would know.” “In the same way, your majesty, when I think of the great disciples who have attained final nibbāna, I know the Blessed One is unsurpassed.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Unsurpassed Nature of the Buddha second

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible to know that the Buddha is unsurpassed?” “Yes, your majesty, it is possible to know that the Blessed One is unsurpassed.” “How, Venerable Nāgasena, is it possible to know that the Buddha is unsurpassed?” “In the past, your majesty, an elder named Tissa was a teacher of writing and many years have passed since he passed away. How is it that he is still known?” “By his writing, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, whoever sees the Dhamma sees the Blessed One, for the Dhamma was taught by the Blessed One.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Knowing the Unsurpassed Nature of the Buddha third

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, have you seen the Dhamma?” “Throughout their lives, your majesty, disciples should proceed with the Buddha as their guide, the Buddha as the one showing the way.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Seeing the Dhamma fourth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is it so that one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects?” “Yes, your majesty, one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects.” “How, Venerable Nāgasena, is it that one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects? Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, if a person kindled one lamp from another would that lamp have transmigrated from the other lamp?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects.” “Give me another analogy.” “Do you remember, your majesty, learning some verse from your teacher of verses?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Then, your majesty, has that verse transmigrated from the teacher?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, one does not transmigrate and yet one reconnects.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Reconnecting and Not Transmigrating fifth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is an experiencer to be found?” The elder responded: “According to ultimate reality, an experiencer is not to be found.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Experiencer sixth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is there any being at all that transmigrates from this body to another body?” “Certainly not, your majesty.” “If, venerable sir, there is no transmigrating from this body to another body, is it not then that one would be freed from evil actions?” “Yes, your majesty, if it would not reconnect, then one would be freed from evil actions. But because, your majesty, it does reconnect, one therefore is not freed from evil actions.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person or other might steal another person’s mangos, would that man deserve punishment?” “Yes, venerable sir, he would deserve punishment.” “But, your majesty, those mangos that were taken are not the same as those that were planted, why would he deserve punishment?” “Those mangos, venerable sir, arose dependent on the others, therefore he would deserve punishment.” “In the same way, your majesty, with this name-and-form one performs a lovely or an evil action, and by this action another name-and-form reconnects. Therefore, one is not freed from evil actions.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Transmigrating to Another Body seventh

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, for a wholesome or unwholesome action done by this name-and-form, where do those actions remain?” “Those actions would follow one, your majesty, like a shadow that never leaves.” “Is it then possible, venerable sir, to point to those actions and say they remain here or there?” “It is not possible, your majesty, to point to those actions and say they remain here or there.” “Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, for those trees where the fruit has not yet arisen, is it possible to point to those fruits and say those fruits remain here or there?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, as long as the continuity of life is not cut off, it is not possible to point to those actions and say they remain here or there.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Existence of the Fruits of Actions eighth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does one who re-arises know, ‘I will re-arise’?” “Yes, your majesty, one who re-arises knows, ‘I will re-arise’.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, when a householder farmer plants seeds in the ground and it rains well, does he know that grain will grow?” “Yes, venerable sir, he would know.” “In the same way, your majesty, one who re-arises knows, ‘I will re-arise’.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Knowing Re-arising ninth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does the Buddha exist?” “Yes, your majesty, the Blessed One exists.” “Is it then possible, venerable sir, to point to the Buddha as being either here or there?” “The Blessed One has passed away, your majesty, in the element of nibbāna without residue remaining, so it is not possible to point to the Blessed One as being either here or there.” “Please give me an analogy.” “What do you think, your majesty, when the flame of a great burning mass of fire has been extinguished, is it possible to point to that flame and say it remains here or there?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, for that flame has ceased and gone beyond description.” “In the same way, your majesty, the Blessed One has passed away in the element of nibbāna without residue remaining, so it is not possible to point to the Blessed One as being either here or there. However, your majesty, it is possible to point out the Blessed One through the body of Dhamma, for this Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Pointing Out the Buddha tenth Buddha Chapter fifth In this chapter ten questions

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the body dear to recluses?” “No, your majesty, the body is not dear to recluses.” “Then, venerable sir, why do you cherish and treasure it?” “But, your majesty, when you have gone into battle have you been struck by arrows from time to time?” “Yes, venerable sir, I have.” “And would the wound, your majesty, be anointed with a salve, smeared with oil, and wrapped in a soft bandage?” “Yes, venerable sir, the wound would be.” “And was the wound dear to you, your majesty, that it was anointed with a salve, smeared with oil, and wrapped in a soft bandage?” “No, venerable sir, the wound was not dear to me, it was for the healing of the flesh that it was anointed with a salve, smeared with oil, and wrapped in a soft bandage.” “In the same way, your majesty, the body is not dear to recluses, but recluses look after the body without attachment for the maintenance of the holy life. And moreover, your majesty, the body is said by the Blessed One to be like a wound, and therefore recluses look after the body as they would a wound without attachment. And this too was said, your majesty, by the Blessed One: ‘Covered with moist skin, the great wound with nine openings Oozes everywhere putrid-smelling secretions.’” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Love of the Body Question first

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the Buddha all-knowing and all-seeing?” “Yes, your majesty, the Buddha is all-knowing and all-seeing.” “Then why, Venerable Nāgasena, did he proclaim the training steps for his disciples gradually?” “But, your majesty, is there some doctor who knows all the medicines on this earth?” “Yes, venerable sir, there is.” “And would that doctor, your majesty, administer medicine to a sick person at the time of being ill or when not ill?” “He would administer medicine to a sick person, venerable sir, at the time of being ill and not when not ill.” “In the same way, your majesty, the Blessed One who is all-knowing and all-seeing did not proclaim a training rule to his disciples at the wrong time, but when the time was right he proclaimed a training rule to his disciples, which is not to be transgressed all life long.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” All-knowing Nature Question second

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, was the Buddha endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person and distinguished with the eighty secondary features, with radiant complexion, skin like gold, and a halo that extends for one fathom?” “Yes, your majesty, he was.” “But, venerable sir, were his mother and father endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person … and a halo that extends for one fathom?” “No, your majesty, they were not.” “That being so, venerable sir, is it not then that the Buddha arose endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person … and a halo that extends for one fathom? But surely a child is like their mother or those on their mother’s side or like their father or those on their father’s side.” The elder said, “But is there, your majesty, any lotus with a hundred leaves?” “Yes, venerable sir, there is.” “And where then is the origin for that?” “It is born from mud and it thrives in water.” “Then, your majesty, is the lotus like the mud in colour, smell, or taste?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Or is it like the water in smell or taste?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “In the same way, your majesty, the Buddha was endowed with the thirty-two characteristics of a great person and distinguished with the eighty secondary features, with radiant complexion, skin like gold, and a halo that extends for one fathom, and his parents were not.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Characteristics of a Great Person Question third

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, was the Buddha a Brahma-farer (celibate)?” “Yes, your majesty, the Buddha was celibate.” “Well then, Venerable Nāgasena, was the Buddha a student of Brahmā?” “But, your majesty, do you have a chief elephant?” “Yes, venerable sir, I do.” “And does this elephant, your majesty, roar the ‘Heron’s roar’ from time to time?” “Yes, venerable sir, he does.” “Well then, your majesty, is this elephant a student of the heron?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Was Brahmā, your majesty, one with intelligence or without?” “With intelligence, venerable sir.” “Well then, your majesty, Brahmā was a student of the Blessed One.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Celibacy of the Blessed One Question fourth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, is the higher ordination good?” “Yes, your majesty, the higher ordination is good.” “But, Venerable Nāgasena, did the Buddha receive the higher ordination or not?” “The Blessed One, your majesty, reached the highest attainment at the foot of the Bodhi tree, together with omniscience. There was no giving of ordination to the Blessed One by others, in the way that the Blessed One proclaimed a training rule to his disciples, which is not to be transgressed all life long.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Higher Ordination of the Blessed One Question fifth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, those who weep on the death of a mother, and those who weep with affection for the Dhamma, for whom of these two weeping are the tears a medicine, and for whom are the tears not a medicine?” “The tears of one, your majesty, are hot and stained with lust, anger, and delusion, and the tears of the other are cool and unstained with rapture and joy. That which is cool, your majesty, is a medicine; that which is hot is not a medicine.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Tears Being a Medicine or Not sixth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the difference between being with attachment and being without attachment?” “One is sticky, your majesty, and the other is not sticky.” “What is the meaning, venerable sir, of ‘sticky’ and ‘not sticky’?” “One is desirable, your majesty, and the other is not desirable.” “As I see it, venerable sir, both the one with attachment and the one without attachment wish for beautiful hard and soft food, and neither wishes for something bad.” “One who is not without attachment, your majesty, eats their food and experiences both the taste and the attachment to the taste. But the one who is without attachment eats their food and experiences just the taste and not the attachment to the taste.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Difference Between Being With Attachment and Without Attachment seventh

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, where does wisdom reside?” “Nowhere, your majesty.” “Then, Venerable Nāgasena, is there no wisdom?” “Where does the wind reside, your majesty?” “Nowhere, venerable sir.” “Then, your majesty, is there no wind?” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on the Establishment of Wisdom eighth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, as to which you said ‘cyclic existence’. What is this cyclic existence?” “Your majesty, that which is born here dies here, and having died here, it arises elsewhere. Then, having been born there it dies there, and having died there, it arises elsewhere. Thus, your majesty, this is cyclic existence.” “Please give me an analogy.” “Just as, your majesty, some person may eat a ripe mango and plant the seed. Then, when it has grown up as a mature mango tree, it would give fruit. And then that man might eat a ripe mango from it and plant the seed and, when it has grown up as a mature mango tree, it too would give fruit. And thus, no end to these mango trees can be discerned. In the same way, your majesty, that which is born here dies here, and having died here, it arises elsewhere. Then, having been born there it dies there, and having died there, it arises elsewhere. Thus, your majesty, this is cyclic existence.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Cyclic Existence ninth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, how does one remember what was done long ago in the past?” “With mindfulness, your majesty.” “Is it not, Venerable Nāgasena, that one remembers with one’s mind and not with mindfulness?” “Do you not know personally, your majesty, about some task you have done and have forgotten?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Then were you, your majesty, on that occasion without a mind?” “Certainly not, venerable sir, on that occasion there was no mindfulness.” “So, why do you say, your majesty, that one remembers with one’s mind and not with mindfulness?” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Remembrance of What was Done Long Ago tenth

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, does all mindfulness arise through knowing directly or does it come with outside help?” “By knowing directly, your majesty, and with outside help.” “If thus, Venerable Nāgasena, all mindfulness is from directly knowing, there is none with outside help.” “If there were no mindfulness with outside help, your majesty, then artisans would have no need for practice, or craftsmanship, or schooling, and teachers would be useless, but since there is mindfulness with outside help, the opposite is true.” “You are clever, Venerable Nāgasena!” Question on Directly Knowing eleventh Mindfulness Chapter sixth In this chapter eleven questions

The king asked: “Venerable Nāgasena, in how many ways does mindfulness arise?” “Your majesty, mindfulness arises in seventeen ways.” “In what seventeen ways?” “Mindfulness arises, your majesty, through knowing directly, with outside help, from consciousness of a substantiality, from consciousness of welfare, from consciousness of misfortune, from a common sign, from an uncommon sign, from understanding due to speech, from a distinguishing characteristic, from remembering, from reckoning, from calculation, from bearing in mind, from mental development, from recording in books, from association of ideas, and from experience. How does mindfulness arise through knowing directly? Just as, your majesty, Venerable Ānanda or the female lay follower Khujjuttarā or those others who remember past births remember a past birth, thus does mindfulness arise through knowing directly. How does mindfulness arise with outside help? If others urge one who is naturally muddled in mindfulness so that he remembers, thus does mindfulness arise with outside help. How does mindfulness arise from consciousness of a substantiality? When there is a consecration into sovereignty or the attainment of the fruit of stream entry, thus does mindfulness arise from consciousness of a substantiality. How does mindfulness arise from consciousness of welfare? One remembers when one was happy, ‘There was happiness because of that.’ Thus, does mindfulness arise from consciousness of welfare.
